q: Matter is made up of tiny particles, which can be atoms or molecules.
e: True. Matter is made up of tiny particles, which can be atoms or molecules. That is how this part of the lesson is stated.

q: Plasma is a hot ionised gas containing charged particles.
e: True. Plasma is a hot ionised gas containing charged particles. In a gas, particles are far apart, move fast, and have weak attractions.

q: The particles in a solid are packed very tightly together with weak forces between one another.
e: False. It is not true that the particles in a solid are packed very tightly together with weak forces between one another. Solid particles are packed tightly with strong forces between them.

q: Solids have a definite shape and volume.
e: True. Solids have a definite shape and volume. That is how this part of the lesson is stated.

q: Unlike gases, solids cannot be compressed and do not flow.
e: True. Unlike gases, solids cannot be compressed and do not flow. That is how this part of the lesson is stated.

q: Solids do not expand when heated.
e: False. It is not true that solids do not expand when heated. Solids usually expand when heated.

q: Liquids are composed of particles which are fixed in definite positions as in solids.
e: False. It is not true that liquids are composed of particles which are fixed in definite positions as in solids. Liquid particles are not locked in place; they can slide past one another.

q: Liquids can have a definite volume because the particles in liquid are held together more strongly than those in gases.
e: True. Liquids can have a definite volume because the particles in liquid are held together more strongly than those in gases. In a liquid, particles touch but can slide, so volume is fixed while shape is not.

q: Unlike gases, liquids cannot be compressed but they can flow easily.
e: True. Unlike gases, liquids cannot be compressed but they can flow easily. That is how this part of the lesson is stated.

q: The particles in a gas are in constant and rapid motion because of strong attractive forces between gaseous particles.
e: False. It is not true that the particles in a gas are in constant and rapid motion because of strong attractive forces between gaseous particles. Gas particles move fast because attractions are weak, not strong.

q: Gases do not have a definite volume and shape of their own.
e: True. Gases do not have a definite volume and shape of their own. That is how this part of the lesson is stated.

q: All gases can easily be compressed and spread in all directions.
e: True. All gases can easily be compressed and spread in all directions. That is how this part of the lesson is stated.

q: Brownian motion is the continuous random movement of small particles suspended in a gas or liquid.
e: True. Brownian motion is the continuous random movement of small particles suspended in a gas or liquid. In a liquid, particles touch but can slide, so volume is fixed while shape is not.

q: Brownian motion arises from collisions with the solid container walls only.
e: False. It is not true that brownian motion arises from collisions with the solid container walls only. Brownian motion comes from collisions with unseen molecules in the fluid.

q: Diffusion is mainly seen in solids and liquids.
e: False. It is not true that diffusion is mainly seen in solids and liquids. Diffusion is fastest and most obvious in gases, though it occurs in other states too.

q: In diffusion, the particles of one substance mix with and move through the particles of another substance.
e: True. In diffusion, the particles of one substance mix with and move through the particles of another substance. Diffusion is the spreading of particles from higher to lower concentration.

q: The bigger the mass of particles, the faster the particles diffuse.
e: False. It is not true that the bigger the mass of particles, the faster the particles diffuse. Heavier particles diffuse more slowly, not faster.

q: The higher the temperature, it enables the particles to diffuse faster.
e: True. The higher the temperature, it enables the particles to diffuse faster. That is how this part of the lesson is stated.

q: The air, the sea water, and alloys are pure substances.
e: False. It is not true that the air, the sea water, and alloys are pure substances. Air, seawater, and alloys are mixtures, not pure substances.

q: Adding sugar to tea or coffee is a solid-liquid mixture.
e: True. Adding sugar to tea or coffee is a solid-liquid mixture. A mixture holds substances together physically, and its composition can vary.

q: A physical change is a change in which no new substances are formed.
e: True. A physical change is a change in which no new substances are formed. A physical change does not make a new substance; melting and boiling are typical examples.

q: Melting, boiling, freezing, evaporation, vaporisation, condensation and sublimation are considered as chemical changes.
e: False. It is not true that melting, boiling, freezing, evaporation, vaporisation, condensation and sublimation are considered as chemical changes. Those state changes are physical, not chemical.

q: The temperature at which a solid melts is called the melting point.
e: True. The temperature at which a solid melts is called the melting point. Melting is solid to liquid as particles gain energy and leave their fixed places.

q: When a solid substance is heated, the particles of the solid vibrate more weakly.
e: False. It is not true that when a solid substance is heated, the particles of the solid vibrate more weakly. Heating makes solid particles vibrate more strongly.

q: Vaporisation is the process that occurs when a chemical or element is converted from a liquid to a vapour.
e: True. Vaporisation is the process that occurs when a chemical or element is converted from a liquid to a vapour. An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom.

q: Evaporation is the process of a substance in a gaseous state changing to a liquid state due to a decrease in temperature.
e: False. It is not true that evaporation is the process of a substance in a gaseous state changing to a liquid state due to a decrease in temperature. Evaporation is liquid becoming vapour, not gas becoming liquid.

q: Boiling is the rapid vaporisation of a liquid, which occurs when a liquid is heated to its boiling point.
e: True. Boiling is the rapid vaporisation of a liquid, which occurs when a liquid is heated to its boiling point. Boiling is liquid to gas throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

q: Sublimation is the change of liquid state directly into gaseous state.
e: False. It is not true that sublimation is the change of liquid state directly into gaseous state. Sublimation is solid going directly to gas, not liquid to gas.

q: Deposition is the direct solidification of a vapour by cooling.
e: True. Deposition is the direct solidification of a vapour by cooling. Vapour is the gas form of a substance that is usually liquid, made by vaporisation.

q: A chemical change is a change in which one or more new substances are formed.
e: True. A chemical change is a change in which one or more new substances are formed. A chemical change makes new substances, like burning or cooking rice.

q: Cooking of rice from rice grains and burning of a match are examples of physical changes.
e: False. It is not true that cooking of rice from rice grains and burning of a match are examples of physical changes. Cooking rice and burning a match are chemical changes because new substances form.

q: Heating of limestone or marble is an example of dissociation or decomposition.
e: True. Heating of limestone or marble is an example of dissociation or decomposition. That is how this part of the lesson is stated.

q: Use of magnesia to treat gastric patient is an example of precipitation.
e: False. It is not true that use of magnesia to treat gastric patient is an example of precipitation. Magnesia treating stomach acid is a neutralization, not precipitation as the main idea.

q: Passing carbon dioxide into lime water is an example of precipitation.
e: True. Passing carbon dioxide into lime water is an example of precipitation. Precipitation is formation of an insoluble solid from a solution.

q: The temperature at which the vapour pressure of the liquid is equal to the atmospheric pressure of the surrounding is called the boiling point.
e: True. The temperature at which the vapour pressure of the liquid is equal to the atmospheric pressure of the surrounding is called the boiling point. Raising temperature or lowering pressure helps a liquid evaporate.

q: Freezing is the process in which a liquid becomes sufficiently cold to change into a solid.
e: True. Freezing is the process in which a liquid becomes sufficiently cold to change into a solid. Freezing is liquid to solid as particles lose energy and lock into place.

q: Condensation is the change from a liquid state to its gaseous state.
e: False. It is not true that condensation is the change from a liquid state to its gaseous state. Condensation is gas to liquid, not liquid to gas.

q: Sublimation is the change of solid state directly into gaseous state without melting.
e: True. Sublimation is the change of solid state directly into gaseous state without melting. Sublimation is solid going straight to gas, or the reverse, without a liquid stage.

q: All samples of matter can be divided into two categories: pure substances and mixtures.
e: True. All samples of matter can be divided into two categories: pure substances and mixtures. A pure substance has a fixed composition, either an element or a compound.

q: A pure substance is a form of matter that always has a variable composition.
e: False. It is not true that a pure substance is a form of matter that always has a variable composition. A pure substance has a fixed composition, not a variable one.

q: John Dalton proposed the theory of matter at the beginning of the 19th century.
e: True. John Dalton proposed the theory of matter at the beginning of the 19th century. Dalton treated atoms as the tiny particles that make up elements.

q: According to John Dalton, atoms were visible and divisible.
e: False. It is not true that according to John Dalton, atoms were visible and divisible. Dalton treated atoms as invisible and indivisible.

q: Modern experimental evidence has shown that atoms are indivisible.
e: False. It is not true that modern experimental evidence has shown that atoms are indivisible. Modern experimental evidence has shown that atoms are divisible.

q: The atom is still considered as the basic unit of any element.
e: True. The atom is still considered as the basic unit of any element. An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom.

q: A molecule is the smallest unit of any substances that possesses the properties of that substance.
e: True. A molecule is the smallest unit of any substances that possesses the properties of that substance. A property is physical if measuring it leaves the substance itself unchanged, and chemical if composition changes.

q: Elements are substances consisting of more than one type of atom.
e: False. It is not true that elements are substances consisting of more than one type of atom. Elements are not substances consisting of more than one type of atom.

q: There are 92 known elements which occur naturally.
e: True. There are 92 known elements which occur naturally. An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom.
